archetype.name: Dual-Threat (developmental)
archetype.definition: A 6-5, 236-pound third-year former sixth-rounder whose legs and occasional intermediate throw are real, but whose pocket operation is so far a long way from starter grade.

report.headline: The legs worked, the pocket didn't: seven sacks buried a promising first start
report.take:
Joe Milton III is the third quarterback to start for Philadelphia this season. Jalen Hurts started six of the first eight weeks and Tanner McKee two, and Milton's lone start, an 11-19 home loss to the Giants, is the only regular-season sample in the dossier. There is no career line behind it. Everything here is one game, 46 dropbacks, and should be read that way. He is QB1 on the depth chart as of November 10, but the dossier doesn't say why Hurts isn't playing or how long this lasts.

The game split cleanly in two. As a runner he was the offense's best play: 64 rushing yards on 9 carries, the top per-game rushing figure among the 49 qualifiers. His 6 scrambles went for 50 yards at +0.508 EPA each, and three of his four designed runs were successful. As a passer he was the worst in the league: -16.9 passing EPA, 49th of 49, a 17.1% sack rate (also 49th) and a CPOE 11.3 points below the league average. Seven sacks on 46 dropbacks, a 3.12-second time to throw and a 27.5% hit-or-sacked rate describe a quarterback holding the ball looking for something downfield and then trying to escape. The scrambles that worked don't come close to paying for the sacks that didn't.

The passing film the numbers suggest isn't hopeless; it's lopsided. Between 10 and 19 air yards he was good: 9 attempts, +0.44 EPA, two-thirds successful, positive CPOE. The breakdown is everywhere a quarterback is supposed to be automatic. Under 10 air yards only 15% of his throws were successful. Screens and throws behind the line lost -0.567 per play, and he was 0 for 4 deep. Third down was the killer: 9.1% conversions at -1.183 EPA a play with three sacks, against an average of 8.1 yards to go. His -1.45 air yards to the sticks says too many of the throws he did get off came up short of the marker. The surrounding cast was thin, too. DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks don't appear among his targets, Darius Cooper cost -0.488 EPA a target, and the offense ranks 29th in EPA and 31st in success rate overall.

The zero interceptions rank first in the league, but that is a one-game artifact rather than a trait. He lost a fumble and threw with 17.6% aggressiveness, so the ball was in danger. What carries forward is the shape of the profile: a big mobile quarterback who can create with his legs and hit the in-breaker, but who hasn't yet shown he can get the ball out on time against pressure. Until the sack rate comes down sharply, his ceiling as a passer is capped no matter what the scrambles add.

strengths.title: Scrambling and designed runs produce
strengths.body: His legs were the only consistently positive part of the offense: 64 yards on the ground and each scramble worth about half a point. At his size, with designed runs succeeding three times in four, this is a repeatable trait rather than luck, though one game can't fix the rate. Expect rushing to keep his floor up even when the passing stalls.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws were on target
strengths.body: Between 10 and 19 air yards he completed two-thirds of his throws, beat expectation and added positive EPA. That window is where his arm and size show up, throwing over linebackers to the sideline and the in-breakers. On nine attempts it's a hint, not a fact, but it's the passing skill most worth building the offense around.

concerns.title: Holding the ball into sacks
concerns.body: Seven sacks, a league-worst 17.1% sack rate and a 3.12-second time to throw point to processing more than protection. Philadelphia's line allows hits at a 23rd-ranked rate, which is below average but not catastrophic. The scrambles are the upside of extending plays, but the sacks, plus a lost fumble, cost far more than the scrambles gained. This is the single number most likely to decide whether he keeps the job.

concerns.title: Short game and third downs failed
concerns.body: The throws that should be easy weren't. Under 10 air yards only 15% were successful, screens lost over half a point each, and third downs converted 9.1% of the time. Missing on rhythm throws is typical of a young quarterback who doesn't trust the first read. A depleted receiver room didn't help, so some of this can improve with reps and with Smith and Wicks back.

concerns.title: Accuracy well below expectation
concerns.body: His CPOE sits 11.3 points under the league average, and he went 0 for 4 on deep balls. Some of that is a thin receiver group, with Cooper at -0.488 EPA a target. But inaccuracy on short throws is on the quarterback, and with no prior seasons there's no track record to argue it's a blip.

trend.note: One start, no path yet: a game of strong running and a few good intermediate throws wrapped around a broken pocket. The bye gives him two weeks of first-team prep before the next data point.

nextGame.headline: Pittsburgh's pass rush targets exactly what broke him
nextGame.body:
Pittsburgh is the wrong defense for a quarterback who takes sacks. It ranks 4th in sack rate and 6th in defensive EPA, and it has held quarterbacks to the 4th-fewest PPR points and allowed the 2nd-fewest touchdowns to the position. It's also stingy on short passes (8th) and against the run (6th in rush EPA allowed), which squeezes both his scramble lanes and the quick game he already struggled with. The openings are deep, where Pittsburgh ranks 23rd in EPA allowed, and over the middle to the tight end, where it is 30th of 32 against TE1s. Dallas Goedert was one of only two Philadelphia targets with positive EPA in Milton's start, so a steady diet of Goedert is the clearest path.

The bigger swing is on his side. DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks, both regular starters by snap share, are listed out with expected returns of November 22, the date of this game. Getting even one back would change a receiver room that had Darius Cooper absorbing eight targets for heavily negative EPA. Pittsburgh's injury list barely touches the matchup: the two cornerbacks out, Echols and Slaughter, are depth pieces by snap share, and Joseph-Day is a part-time interior lineman. The extra rest after the bye is the one structural edge Milton has.

keyMatchups.title: Steelers rush vs. long time to throw
keyMatchups.body: A defense sacking quarterbacks at the 4th-best rate meets a passer who took sacks on 17.1% of dropbacks and held the ball over three seconds. Unless the plan shortens his reads with play-action, under center and quick game, the sack count could stay ugly. Watch the first third-and-long.

keyMatchups.title: Goedert against a soft TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh allows the third-most EPA per play to opposing top tight ends, and Goedert added positive EPA on his six targets last time. Seam and intermediate throws to the tight end fit the one zone where Milton played well.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots vs. a leaky back end
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh ranks 23rd in deep-pass EPA allowed, so the shots are there to be taken. Milton went 0 for 4 deep against the Giants, though, so it's an opening he has to prove he can hit.

nextGame.watch: Whether Smith or Wicks is active, and whether Milton's sack count drops below the seven he took against the Giants.

restOfSeason.body:
Assuming he holds the job, the rushing is the most sustainable part: his size and the scramble results suggest roughly 30 to 55 rushing yards a game is reasonable even as defenses adjust. The sack rate should come down from 17.1%, simply because almost nobody sustains that, but the long time to throw suggests he stays well above the league average of 7.3%. That means 3 to 5 sacks a game, not 7. The passing should improve modestly with Smith and Wicks back and with more first-team reps, though the short-game inaccuracy and lack of any track record make a jump to league-average efficiency unlikely this year. Expect 150 to 210 passing yards a game, touchdowns coming slowly in an offense that ranks 29th in EPA, and interceptions appearing eventually; the zero won't hold.

The largest variable isn't on the field. Philadelphia has already started three quarterbacks, and the dossier gives no reason for Hurts' absence or a timeline for it. A return by Hurts or a turn back to McKee ends this sample at any point. Fantasy managers should treat him as a rushing-floor streamer in good matchups, not a weekly starter.
swingFactors: Whether he keeps the starting job
Return of DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks
Cutting the sack rate by getting the ball out on time

confidence.note: One start, 46 dropbacks, no prior career data, and an unclear QB situation.
